the Canadian public service is in a period of rapid change and development, that the pace of change has been accelerating since the late 1960s, and that there are many indications that the Service will be even more different in the future than it is today.

(1) the Canadian public service is a large, complex and highly differentiated organization, with a wide variety of roles and tasks, and (2) the public service is not a single, monolithic, undifferentiated organization.

the Canadian system of central agencies and departments has been reformed in a way which, while preserving the traditional Westminster model, has moved it in the direction of the American model, which has been described as a “presidential” model.

the Canadian public service has been transformed from one in which the departments were largely autonomous to a highly centralised one, in which the centre exercises tight control over the departments.
the reforms of the 1960s and early 1970s were designed to make the Service more effective, more accountable and more efficient.

the Service has been transformed from an administrative to a managerial system, and that the transformation has been accompanied by a significant shift in emphasis from the political to the bureaucratic level of the system.
